item.title: Serve Robotics opens robot delivery network for others to build on
item.dc:creator: The Robot Report Staff
item.description:
Serve Robotics says its on-demand delivery API allows third parties to develop new delivery services on its fleet of more than 2,000 robots.

The post Serve Robotics opens robot delivery network for others to build on appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
The AV Delivery Developer Portal enables anyone to call robots from Serve’s delivery fleet. Source: Serve Robotics

Serve Robotics Inc. today launched the AV Delivery Developer Portal, which it said gives developers, businesses, hobbyists, and AI assistants the opportunity to programmatically summon its sidewalk delivery robots. The company said its public application programming interface, or API, allows others to work with its autonomous robot fleet. It also released a sandbox environment where anyone can build and test applications before using them with live robots.

“You shouldn’t have to start a robotics company to build something useful with robots,” stated Ali Kashani, co-founder and CEO of Serve Robotics. “We’ve spent years figuring out how robots can navigate neighborhoods. The people who live and work there will have needs we haven’t thought of. Opening our fleet gives us an opportunity to serve those needs.”

Spun out of Uber in 2021, Serve Robotics designs and operates robots that autonomously navigate complex, human-centric environments. The Redwood City, Calif.-based company said it has deployed more than 2,000 robots across the U.S. and Australia, reaching about 3 million people and supporting delivery for more than 4,000 restaurants.

Earlier this year, Serve acquired hospital service robot provider Diligent Robotics. Serve asserted that it designs its robot hardware and software to work safely in public and private environments at scale.

Serve Robotics opens tech to new robots, developers

Serve Robotics said its mobile robots are intended to make daily errands easy and on-demand delivery affordable and accessible. Businesses can use the robots to transport goods between their offices, and local businesses can expand their delivery footprints without hiring more staffers, the company noted.

Last week, Serve launched Serve Physical AI Services, opening its technology to companies building new types of robots. While the company’s systems have completed hundreds of thousands of deliveries across more than 150 neighborhoods in 20 U.S. cities, they have been available only through third-party delivery partners — until now.

Today, Serve said it “opens the fleet itself to anyone needing affordable and efficient autonomous last-mile delivery.” Developers can build on their existing apps, businesses can add robots into their daily workflows, and AI assistants can carry out tasks in the physical world, it said.

The AV Delivery Developer Portal allows anyone to dispatch those robots with a few lines of code or even an AI agent. “The same robots previously only available through the largest delivery platforms can now power any local delivery,” said Serve Robotics.

Submit your innovation now!

Builders can use API and sandbox before live robots

“Building on the fleet works like building on any other API,” claimed Serve Robotics. An application or AI assistant can request a pickup and dropoff, confirm the details, and tracks a robot until the delivery is complete. Serve handles the dispatch, routing, navigation, and remote supervision to ensure a timely, safe, and reliable delivery.

Deliveries are limited to Serve’s active service areas and operating hours, as well as to items that fit within the robot’s cargo compartment.

The sandbox lets developers simulate robots, run delivery workflows, and rehearse edge cases before running real robots. Builders can explore the documentation and sandbox at https://developer.serverobotics.com.

Access to live robots is subject to Serve’s approval. Those who wish to move beyond the sandbox can indicate their interest via the portal, said the company.

The post Serve Robotics opens robot delivery network for others to build on appeared first on The Robot Report.

item.title: Memories.ai builds standardized egocentric video pipeline
item.dc:creator: Mike Oitzman
item.description:
Memories.ai provides standardized egocentric video collection and AI-powered annotation to build training data infrastructure for robotics.

The post Memories.ai builds standardized egocentric video pipeline appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Memories.ai models label every clip: Memories-H0 for hand pose, EgoAction for action segments. | Credit: Memories.ai

Memories.ai is building a data pipeline for robotics companies that combines standardized video collection with AI-powered annotation to turn everyday egocentric footage into training data for robots.

The San Francisco-based company is developing software and AI to help robots understand the physical world. It builds video-understanding models and data infrastructure, and it collects and annotates first-person (egocentric) video to provide high-quality training data to robotics companies.

The longer-term aim is to be a data-infrastructure partner for robotics and physical AI, not just a data vendor.

Memories.ai builds platform on video data

Memories.ai claimed that its video data infrastructure platform is built for physical AI, robotics, world models, vision-language-action (VLA) models, and humanoids. It provides a curated video data lake featuring egocentric video, along with custom annotation services and dataset tools to train robot learning models.

The company obtains egocentric video through data collectors and partners, providing them with standardized capture hardware—described as a modular camera setup—and uniform process to collect footage in a consistent way.

Memories.ai then processes and annotates the data with its models and makes it available through its data infrastructure. The company has published multiple elements of its research on its GitHub repo. It has also published at the ICLR, NeurIPS, and EMNLP events.

Submit your innovation now!

NVIDIA Cosmos helps realize physical AI vision

“Our vision right now is to accelerate physical intelligence, and our vision is to stand really at the frontier to being able to be part of the robotics game,” Shawn Shen, co-founder and CEO of Memories.ai, recently told The Robot Report. “We really bring robotics into the actual physical world, and I believe that’s our whole team’s vision. And whatever can help us to make that vision come faster, we’re happy to do it.”

Shen said the company is focused on processing its own data, rather than collecting video from a wide range of devices and sources. Once it gets data from partners, Memories.ai processes and annotates the footage itself.

The company said last month that it has used NVIDIA Cosmos to interpret video entering its data lake. It then curates that data to post-train Cosmos for customers’ robotics and industrial applications. This loop turns real-world video into models tailored to the tasks our customers need to solve.

Pipeline has a modular design

Memories.ai said its setup is modular to support diverse tasks and camera views. Shen asserted that the company wants to grow with the industry as AI models mature for more robotics applications.

“We want to be long-term partners,” he said. “We don’t want to just sell you the data. In the future, we want to work with you on the models. We want to work with you on the infra because we know that you are, and will be, limited by your resources too.”

For robotics customers, Memory AI plans to tailor the data to their needs, offer exclusive or non-exclusive arrangements, and potentially expand its role into models and video infrastructure.

The post Memories.ai builds standardized egocentric video pipeline appeared first on The Robot Report.

item.title: Can AI agents program industrial robots without training data? Berkeley says yes
item.dc:creator: Mike Oitzman
item.description:
UC Berkeley and NVIDIA have released open-source tools for teams of AI coding agents that write, simulate, and refine readable robot programs. 

The post Can AI agents program industrial robots without training data? Berkeley says yes appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
The new RoboSimStudio is an open-source project that enables agentic AI coding of robotic simulation environments. | Credit: UC Berkeley

UC Berkeley and NVIDIA have released open-source tools for a new approach: enabling teams of AI coding agents to write, simulate, and refine readable robot programs.

Since the early days of industrial robots, programming, tuning, and troubleshooting robotic workcells has taken weeks to months. New research coming out of UC Berkeley has demonstrated that new agentic AI programming tools could change how industrial robots are coded and maintained.

Why is this important? As anyone who’s programmed an industrial workcell knows, implementing the code has to wait until the end of the design and fabrication process. The robot needs to be installed in the workcell; all of the feeders, conveyance, and other elements also need to be installed. The pressure to get this done all falls on the software team, often when the project deadline is looming.

The new toolset goes beyond the idea of “vibe coding” a robot application. While it generates code with large language models (LLMs), what’s novel is the use of AI agents to manage the coding, testing and deployment.

“Agentic robotics is a fundamental shift in how robots are programmed,” said Ken Goldberg, the William S. Floyd Jr. Distinguished Chair in Engineering at UC Berkeley. “Instead of collecting massive amounts of data and hand-tuning every behavior, teams of agents can quickly generate, test, and refine robot programs that allow human engineers to interpret how the programs work for fine-tuning and verification.”

Researchers introduce GaP and VABAR

  • Graph-as-Policy (GaP) is a modular framework that splits a task into skills — perception, grasp planning, collision-free motion — which agents generate, connect and rehearse in simulation.
  • Variational Automation Benchmark for Agentic Robotics (VABAR) is a benchmark of six tasks: tool sorting, tool hanging, gear meshing, syringe packing, cable insertion, and cable routing. It is built built on Isaac Lab-Arena and Newton, with standardized variations and difficulty tiers.
  • The UC Berkeley and NVIDIA team presented the concept at CoRL 2026 this week in Austin, Texas.

How the toolset works

Dr. Goldberg described the research to The Robot Report. In September, Eric Chen, one of his graduate students, give GPT-6 Astra Eric’s new RoboSimStudio tool to see if it could generate not just a graphic model, but also a full 3D simulation of a scene. And that’s exactly what happened.

According to Goldberg, Chen gave the model a video and this new tool, and within an hour, it had generated a Newton simulation that was incredibly similar to the video.

“When a new frontier model came out in early September, they gave it the tool and a video,” said Goldberg. “Within about an hour, it produced a Newton simulation closely matching the video, by iterative trial and error.”

“And Newton [simulation] is really wonderful,” he added. “The problem is Newton is very complicated. It has a lot of parameters, hundreds of parameters. So generally, people didn’t really use it that much because it’s just too complicated, too many dials and switches.”

Goldberg praised Chen for pulling this together. Initially, Chen built the tool just for himself.

“I want my student Eric to get credit for this,” he said. “He basically sat down and built a new interface for Newton called RoboSimStudio. It is basically just an interface that makes you have sliders on the right-hand side of your screen, and you have a visualizer on the left. … You can tune all these parameters much easier than you could before, so he built that just for himself to make the simulation part easier.”

But simulation alone isn’t enough, according to Goldberg. Simulation matters to the whole approach of using agents to code robots.

“The agent needs a simulator to be able to basically iterate and see how to improve this code,” he said. Goldberg noted that the existing tools “were not very reliable and had a lot of problems.”

The harness converts a VA task specification into a computation graph, optimizes it via self-learning in simulation, and hands G* to an edge-based interpreter that drives the robot — sim and real feedback close the loop. | Credit: UC Berkeley

Agents write and test code

Agentic robotics operates in a loop: Agents write robot code, test it in simulation, see where it fails, and revise. That loop is only as good as the simulator behind it.

Newton Physics, the open-source physics engine that UC Berkeley chose, is powerful but exposes hundreds of parameters, which has kept many developers from using it.

RoboSim Studio made those parameters tractable, and that turned the simulator from a bottleneck into something an AI agent could tune on its own.

UC Berkeley developed the VABAR benchmark suite with NVIDIA Isaac Lab-Arena open-source policy-evaluation framework and the Newton physics engine. It includes a detailed physics-based simulation for contact-rich robot-object interactions.

VABAR evaluates how robots perform on practical manipulation tasks ranging from tool sorting and handing to cable insertion and routing. The tool facilitates comparisons and measures progress across realistic industrial tasks, changing conditions, and increasing levels of difficulty.

Each task includes standardized variations, difficulty tiers, and success metrics, allowing researchers to measure progress, compare approaches, and evaluate whether systems can handle the demands of industrial operation. At the same time, Isaac Lab-Arena enables large-scale systematic evaluations across changing task conditions.

Spencer Huang, director of product for robotics at NVIDIA (and son of CEO Jensen Huang), has worked with Goldberg’s lab at UC Berkeley to interface with the NVIDIA product teams.

The partners listed some of the new capabilities:

  • Graph structure: Each node (perception, grasp, motion planning) can be assigned to its own agent, so agents work in parallel without “stepping on each other’s toes.”
  • ROS equivalence: The graph turns out to be equivalent to a ROS graph and can be converted to ROS 2.
  • Output: Python that calls existing vendor modules (such as KUKA) for low-level drive control. It does not replace robot controllers.
  • The harness: Thousands of prompts and structures constrain the agents.

How do agents change robot programming?

When asked how this new approach differs from straight “vibe coding” of an app, Goldberg responded that the magic is in the harness provided by GaP. The graph structure organizes the agents.

The code produced by “vibe coding” is already mature and well understood, he explained. The use of AI to write code is accepted in software engineering today. But rarely does an application function as intended in the first pass.

This is true for software from human engineers, and it’s equally true for software development developed with AI. Testing and iteration are needed to optimize the application, said Goldberg.

When applied to robotics, the best practice now is to test in simulation before deploying the code on a real robot. With agentic AI, a robotics engineer can enable the agent to iterate on both the simulation environment and then the subsequent code to more efficiently develop the robotic application.

For instance, Bosch is evaluating agentic robotics for diverse industrial automation scenarios. “Agentic robotics holds great promise because it generates interpretable code that engineers can thoroughly analyze before production deployment,” said Liu Ren, senior vice president and AI fellow at Bosch Research. “Bosch Research is actively collaborating with Goldberg and Huang and their teams.”

“AI-powered industrial robots must continuously improve reliability and performance,” said Jeff Mahler, co-founder and chief technology officer of Ambi Robotics. “Agentic robotics converted production data into robot behavior updates, increasing throughput across our U.S. fleet while keeping engineers in control.”

Goldberg is also an advisor to Ambi Robotics.

Submit your innovation now!

The post Can AI agents program industrial robots without training data? Berkeley says yes appeared first on The Robot Report.

item.title: Dynamic Creatures partners with Sixth Wall Studio to bring Hasbro characters to life with robots
item.dc:creator: Brianna Wessling
item.description:
The companies will combine Sixth Wall’s character authoring and alignment with Dynamic Creatures’ mobile, expressive robots.

The post Dynamic Creatures partners with Sixth Wall Studio to bring Hasbro characters to life with robots appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
On the left, Roberta Thomson, the CEO of Sixth Wall Studio, and on the right, Marc Theerman, co-founder and CEO of Dynamic Creatures. | Source: Dynamic Creatures

Dynamic Creatures today said it has partnered with Sixth Wall Studio, an AI studio launched by Hasbro in June 2026. The collaborators plan to bring Hasbro characters to life through interactive robots.

The company will combine its mobile, expressive robots with Sixth Wall‘s character authoring and alignment. The goal is to create characters that can greet guests, share adventures with them, and remember them when they return at theme parks, resorts, and other entertainment and hospitality venues.

“Today CharacterOS is focused on voice, and Dynamic Creatures is focused on the physical embodiment,” Marc Theermann, the co-founder and CEO of Dynamic Creatures, told The Robot Report. “Together, the partners will work on turning bits and bytes into real personality over time. One of the research areas is to turn answers into meaningful expressions.”

Through the partnership, Sixth Wall Studio will extend its CharacterOS platform and Behavioral Licensing framework into physical experiences. It will support how characters speak, behave and remain true to their established personalities and stories.

Dynamic Creatures said its robots will give that intelligence a physical presence. The company connects a character’s conversation and personality with expressive movements, gazes, gestures, reactions, and more.

“Bringing a character to life means preserving the personality, voice, and story that fans love while opening up new ways to interact,” said Roberta Thomson, CEO of Sixth Wall Studio. “Our partnership with Dynamic Creatures takes that ambition into the physical world. We envision characters that can share an adventure with you while feeling unmistakably authentic from the first hello.”

Dynamic Creatures designed its first character robot, Hugo, to move freely through guest environments. | Source: Dynamic Creatures

Partners plan to use robots to provide better guest experiences

Together, the companies envision encounters that become part of a continuing story. A character at a resort could welcome a guest, send them on a quest and, during a later encounter, ask how the adventure went. 

“One use case we are exploring is for a guest to show the robot their entrance ticket,” Theerman said. “This would allow the robot to identify the guest, and provide personalized experiences such as dining recommendations, or skip the line suggestions.”

Beyond theme parks and resorts, the partners envision applications across hotels, cruise ships, retail destinations, and other immersive environments. Memory-enabled experiences would be developed around guest choice and clearly defined permissions, with deployment details established for each venue and use case. Initial Sixth Wall applications would align with its focus on audiences ages 13 and older.

“Safety is a central pillar for both Dynamic Creatures and Hasbro,” said Theerman. “For Hasbro, it’s about safe interactions, and for Dynamic Creatures, it’s about physical safety of the robot. One way to ensure this today is by having a human in the loop. Over time, more autonomy features will be swapped in, and the human supervisor will go from teleoperation to telemonitoring.”

Dynamic Creatures has a busy few months since emerging from stealth

Dynamic Creatures emerged from stealth in September 2026 and is developing fully custom robots and character experiences built on existing robotic platforms. As Boston Dynamics’ official hospitality and entertainment partner, the Cambridge, Mass.-based company combines advanced mobility with character design and real-time interaction for guest environments.

Its SnowJay robotics AI platform coordinates perception, movement, and behavior, bringing together conversation, memory, facial expressions, and animatronics. The company recently released Hugo, its first living character robot. The robot runs on SnowJay and features 43 actuators.

“For generations, people have formed powerful connections with fictional characters. Now those characters can share our physical world and respond to us as individuals,” said Marc Theermann, co-founder and CEO of Dynamic Creatures. “Sixth Wall brings the character intelligence and creative framework. We bring the physical expression and presence. Together, we want to make meeting a favorite character feel like the beginning of an ongoing relationship.”

item.title: Why predictive maintenance matters more as factories add robots
item.dc:creator: Rob Carbone
item.description:
As robotics scales across industries, companies need a maintenance strategy to collect and use the right data to minimize downtime.

The post Why predictive maintenance matters more as factories add robots appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Robot data combined with predictive analytics can improve uptime and productivity, says ATS. Source: Pexels, Advanced Technology Services

Factories are adding more robots because they can handle repetitive, precise, and physically demanding work at high speed. As robotics take on a greater share of production, keeping those systems available becomes more important.

The International Federation of Robotics (IFR) reported about 5 million industrial robots in operation worldwide in 2025, up 11% from the prior year.

An unexpected robot failure can affect more than one machine. It can interrupt a cell, slow a line, and create delays that spread through the plant. As manufacturers rely more heavily on robotic systems, the need to identify developing problems before they force equipment offline becomes increasingly valuable. 

Why robotic systems raise the support stakes

Traditional preventive maintenance follows a schedule based on time, usage, or manufacturer recommendations. That approach still has value, but it may not reveal what’s happening inside a robot between planned service intervals. A joint, reducer, motor, or controller can begin to show signs of wear while the robot is still operating. 

 Predictive maintenance uses equipment data to identify changes that may point to developing faults. NIST describes condition monitoring as the detection, diagnosis or prediction of faults and failures in industrial equipment. 

For robotics, that means maintenance decisions can be based more on actual equipment condition than on a calendar alone.

Submit your innovation now!

What predictive maintenance can monitor 

Industrial automation and related systems generate many types of operating data. Useful signals depend on the robot, application, and failure mode. Common examples include vibration, temperature, and motor current. Torque, controller alarms, cycle data, and maintenance history can also provide useful context. 

The goal isn’t to collect every available data point. Teams need data that can reveal changes tied to the way a robot operates. A rise in vibration may point to a mechanical issue, while changes in motor current or torque may indicate added resistance or abnormal loading. Temperature variations can also signal that a component isn’t operating as expected. 

Changes in an end effector, sensor, conveyor, or surrounding process can affect robot performance. Looking at the robot in the context of a larger workcell can help teams separate normal operating variation from a change that may deserve maintenance attention. That distinction is especially important if the same robot handles different loads, speeds, or motion paths. 

This is where reliability monitoring can help. Sensors and connected systems can gather machine data, while monitoring and analytics tools help identify changes in equipment behavior. When a pattern changes, maintenance teams can then investigate the cause before a failure forces the robot offline.

Changes in equipment performance, plus environmental or process data, can provide warning of problems, says ATI. Source: Pexels, Advanced Technology Services

Turn robot data into maintenance decisions

Collecting data is only the first step. The information has to support a practical maintenance decision. A useful alert should help a team determine what needs attention, how urgent the issue is, and when the robot can be inspected without causing an unnecessary production interruption. 

This becomes more important as factories operate larger fleets of robots. Maintenance teams may not have time to inspect every asset at the same frequency. Predictive maintenance can help direct attention toward equipment showing signs of change while allowing healthy assets to remain in service. 

Earlier warnings can also improve parts planning. If a component shows signs of deterioration, teams may have more time to confirm the problem, locate the correct replacement part, and schedule work during a planned maintenance window.

Earlier warnings can reduce downtime and improve productivity, says ATS. Source: Pexels, Advanced Technology Services

Getting ahead on productivity, asset life, and safety

The value of predictive maintenance goes beyond preventing unplanned stops. Finding issues early on can limit secondary damage and help manufacturers get more useful life from robotic assets. Planned repairs can also reduce the disruption that occurs when technicians must troubleshoot a failed robot during production. 

A planned maintenance window gives teams more control over when equipment is taken offline and serviced. That can support safer maintenance practices because technicians can prepare for the work instead of responding to an unexpected failure under production pressure. 

As more factories rely heavily on robotics, maintenance strategies need to account for how those systems perform throughout their service life. Predictive maintenance gives manufacturers a way to use equipment data, condition signals and analytics to identify developing issues earlier. When that information leads to timely inspection and repair, manufacturers can reduce unplanned downtime, protect robotic assets and keep production schedules more stable. 

About the author

Rob Carbone is vice president of operations at Advanced Technology Services. He is responsible for leading initiatives that help manufacturers improve equipment reliability, maintenance excellence, and customer success.

The post Why predictive maintenance matters more as factories add robots appeared first on The Robot Report.

item.title: Intel and Altera expand collaboration to simplify sensor integration for physical AI
item.dc:creator: The Robot Report Staff
item.description:
Altera and Intel are working to make it easier to connect diverse sensors, turn data into real-time insights, and develop robotics.

The post Intel and Altera expand collaboration to simplify sensor integration for physical AI appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Altera and Intel are collaborating to accelerate the development of intelligent systems across industries.

Intel Corp. and Altera Corp. today said they are jointly developing flexible, real-time, sensor-bridge reference systems for edge and physical AI applications including robotics. By combining Intel compute, connectivity, and software with Altera field-programmable gate arrays or FPGAs, the companies said they aim to help manufacturers address the growing complexity of connecting, processing, and acting on real-world data across increasingly sensor-rich environments.

“Physical AI systems have to sense, decide, and act in real time, and the physical world demands accuracy, reliability, and safety,” stated Farhad Shafai, head of business solutions and marketing at Altera. “Altera FPGAs provide the sensor connectivity, data processing, and deterministic control that machines need to respond to the physical world, and they stay programmable as sensors and AI models evolve. Combining that with Intel’s compute and software is intended to give OEMs a flexible foundation to tailor systems to their needs.’

Founded in 1983, Altera provides high-performance, programmable compute and connectivity systems for a wide range of advanced and AI-enabled technologies. The San Jose, Calif.-based company claimed that it
is “the largest pure-play FPGA provider with a full-spectrum portfolio serving applications ranging from data centers and communications networks to critical embedded systems.”

Intel acquired Altera for $16.7 billion in 2015 and sold 51% of the company to Silver Lake last year.

Sensor-rich edge environments pose challenges for AI

“Edge and physical AI systems can require data from different sensors and interfaces to be brought together while meeting requirements for timing, performance, power and cost,” said Intel and Altera. “Some applications also require very high bandwidth or flexible form factors in which input/output (I/O) is located away from the compute board. Sensor data must then be streamed rapidly into memory for the host Intel processor to use across edge, robotics and other workloads.”

The companies said they plan to develop modular reference systems that combine Altera programmable hardware with a consistent Intel compute and software foundation. Their goal is to give equipment OEMs greater flexibility as applications, sensors, and workloads evolve, while helping them move more efficiently from prototype to deployment.

“As sensors multiply at the edge and through physical AI systems, our customers need a simpler way to turn real-world data into timely action,” said Dan Rodriguez, corporate vice president and general manager of the Edge Computing Group at Intel. “Together with Altera, we aim to give OEMs a flexible foundation that simplifies integration and helps them move faster from prototype to market deployment while meeting their needs across performance, power and cost.”

Submit your innovation now!

Altera, Intel to apply programmable, real-time processing

Intel and Altera said they plan to address multiple markets where real-time processing and programmable computing matter most. The companies intend to make resulting reference solutions accessible to developers through Intel’s Open Edge Platform software development kit (SDK) and an Altera SDK.

  • Robotics: The partners said they will combine Intel compute, connectivity, and robotics software with Altera FPGAs to address the increasingly complex sensing, timing, and real-time processing requirements of intelligent machines.
  • Healthcare: The companies are jointly developing a reference system targeting the stringent latency and real-time requirements of advanced healthcare equipment.
  • Aerospace and defense: Intel and Altera are collaborating to support next-generation mission systems, with a focus on size, weight, and power requirements for converged AI and signal-processing workloads.

Together, Intel and Altera said they will help OEMs move faster from prototype by reducing integration complexity and addressing performance, power, and cost requirements across a range of edge applications.

The post Intel and Altera expand collaboration to simplify sensor integration for physical AI appeared first on The Robot Report.

item.title: Axon invests $1.2B into Skydio and becomes its U.S. public safety distributor
item.dc:creator: The Robot Report Staff
item.description:
The partners plan to bring Skydio drones to public safety agencies across the U.S. as Axon expands its Drone as First Responder program.

The post Axon invests $1.2B into Skydio and becomes its U.S. public safety distributor appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
The X10 drone features high-resolution visual and radiometric cameras in modular sensor packages. | Source: Skydio

Axon Enterprise Inc. last week said it has invested $1.2 billion in Skydio Inc., a San Mateo, Calif.-based drone manufacturer. With the investment, Axon gains 20% ownership of Skydio, which is valued at $5.2 billion.

Axon will also become Skydio’s exclusive distributor for public safety in the U.S. and Canada. The companies said they are partnering to bring Skydio drones to public safety agencies across the U.S. Axon is also expanding its Drone as First Responder (DFR) program.

“Within a decade, millions of drones will be working across America. Skydio is positioned to lead in every sector they touch,” stated Rick Smith, the founder and CEO of Axon. “Axon is taking a major stake in one of the most valuable categories in tech, and Skydio stays free to move fast. With exclusive channel rights, Axon will widen its lead in public safety drones as Skydio builds the future of American aerial robotics. Two companies, each the best at what it does, will build something far bigger than either could alone.”

Skydio said it serves more than 1,500 public safety customers. Now, more than 28 million Americans live within two miles of a DFR dock. Founded in 2014, the company claimed that it uses AI-backed autonomy to create drones that are easier to operate, safer to fly, and more capable in complex environments.

Skydio DFR gives first responders earlier visibility

At agencies deploying Skydio DFR, priority response times have been reduced by as much as 65%, said Scottsdale, Ariz.-based Axon. Drones arrive before officers on about 80% of the calls where they are deployed.

That earlier visibility can support safer responses, help de-escalate potentially deadly situations, locate missing children and other vulnerable people, and improve outcomes when every second matters, asserted the company.

“Axon has been an incredible partner in bringing our drones to public safety customers across the U.S.,” said Adam Bry, CEO of Skydio. “We’re excited to deepen that partnership with Axon becoming our exclusive channel for U.S. and Canadian public safety. This investment strengthens our ability to accelerate our technology roadmap, scale our impact in public safety, and continue advancing autonomous flight across every critical industry we serve.”

Axon estimated the total addressable market for DFR at approximately $13 billion in the U.S. and Canada alone. That opportunity is already translating into significant commercial momentum, noted the companies. Skydio said its business is growing rapidly, and it expects about $1 billion in total bookings in its current fiscal year.

Axon’s investment consists of approximately $1.2 billion including a mix of cash and Axon stock. The investment includes both primary capital to Skydio and the purchase of shares from existing Skydio shareholders. Skydio plans to use a portion of the cash consideration as growth capital to accelerate innovation, expand its product portfolio, and bring new drone capabilities to customers faster.

Axon said it expects the transactions comprising the investment to close in the fourth quarter of 2026 and first quarter of 2027. The deal is still subject to customary closing conditions.

Skydio isn’t the only drone provider bringing in big funding rounds. Last week, Zipline, which provides delivery drones, raised $1.5 billion in funding. Zipline said it will use the capital to expand its U.S. manufacturing facilities and hire staffers as it builds a nationwide drone delivery network.

item.title: NVIDIA launches GR00T 2 and Isaac Lab 3.0 at CoRL
item.dc:creator: The Robot Report Staff
item.description:
NVIDIA also gave a look at how its partners, like Ambi Robotics, FieldAI, Flexion, Skild AI, RLWRLD, and more, are using these technologies. 

The post NVIDIA launches GR00T 2 and Isaac Lab 3.0 at CoRL appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
A range of developers, including RLWRLD, Skild AI, and Flexion, are already using NVIDIA’s latest technology. | Source: NVIDIA

NVIDIA Corp. today introduced GR00T 2, its updated open frontier world action model, and Isaac Lab 3.0, the latest version of its open-source robot learning framework. The company made these announcements at the Conference on Robot Learning, or CoRL, in Austin, Texas.

NVIDIA also gave a look at how its partners, like Ambi Robotics, Bosch Research, Dexmate, Dyna Robotics, FieldAI, Flexion, Noitom Robotics, Siemens, Skild AI, RLWRLD, UC Berkeley, Walden Robotics, and the University of Washington, are using these technologies.

In addition, NVIDIA hosted the MSIT-NVIDIA AI Startup Partnership Forum at COEX. There, the company announced an investment in South Korean startup Point2, with additional investments planned in Motif Technologies, RLWRLD, and Upstage.

This week is a precarious time for NVIDIA. Yesterday, the company‘s board opened an investigation into co-founder and CEO Jensen Huang. This was in response to Huang acknowledging to the NVIDIA board that he had an intimate relationship with a business executive that U.S. intelligence determined to be a Chinese spy.

In a statement, the board said it has “no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised.”

NVIDIA steps up its world action model with GR00T 2

NVIDIA said it trained GR00T 2 on diverse robot and human data. The model includes 100,000 hours of NVIDIA open-source egocentric data and is intended to enables robot to learn dexterous manipulation skills.

Key features include:

  • Out-of-the-box performance: GR00T 2 completed 40 of 50 evaluated tasks at least once without task-specific demonstrations.
  • Skill transfer: It learns from human demonstrations and transfers skills between different robot bodies without robot demonstrations
  • Generalization with little data: The model achieved 71% average success across 50 tasks with just one demonstration per task, increasing to 95% with five.
  • Agent control: AI agents can use GR00T 2’s application programming interface (API) and supporting tools to run skills in sequence and recover from errors.

GR00T 2 currently ranks among the top three models across all vision-language-action (VLA) and world action model categories for the RoboCasa365, RoboLab, RoboDojo, and MolmoSpaces benchmarks, with multiple leaderboard wins, claimed NVIDIA.

The company asserted that its open workflows and models equip researchers with better tools for data collection and annotation. For researchers building robot-training datasets, NVIDIA’s new open Video to Data workflow turns human video into simulated robot demonstrations, with a challenge inviting researchers to advance it.

The NVIDIA EgoHand open model reconstructs 3D hand motion, trained with data from Noitom Robotics.

Nexuni is testing GR00T 2 for robotic laundry. Foxconn is applying GR00T 2 to factory automation for server manufacturing, and Siemens is evaluating it across industrial use cases.

MicroAGI is using GR00T 2, post-trained through reinforcement learning, to perform Ethernet cable swapping with a YAM robotic arm. Its agentic robotics approach automates the creation and calibration of simulation environments using Isaac Lab 3.0 and Newton, where the policy is trained.

Isaac Lab 3.0 provides the foundation for simulation training

Its latest release, Isaac Lab 3.0, allows researchers to use agents to quickly set up training environments with simulation-ready assets, switch between NVIDIA PhysX and Newton physics solvers, choose renderers for perception-based training, and apply a new reinforcement post-training library to foundation models such as GR00T.

Accurate physics is critical to transferring learned skills from simulation to the real robot, noted NVIDIA. Tighter integration with Newton, an open-source physics engine, now allows Isaac Lab to model deformable objects such as cables and cloth, along with complex articulated systems such as robotic hands with many interacting joints.

Together, Isaac Lab and Newton combine accurate physics with scale to enable researchers to train thousands of simulated robots in parallel. In a vision-based dexterous manipulation benchmark, Isaac Lab 3.0 with Newton reportedly achieved up to 2.5x the training throughput of Isaac Lab 2.3 with PhysX.

NVIDIA introduces new industrial benchmarks for robotics

Learning a skill is one challenge. Performing it reliably across changing conditions is another. NVIDIA’s Isaac Lab-Arena is an open-source framework for scaled policy evaluations. Isaac Lab-Arena enables developers to compose diverse and repeatable evaluations, then run policies across thousands of variations in parallel.

Analyses expose which conditions cause failures, so researchers know what to fix in their next training runs. NVIDIA released the developer preview of Version 0.4, at CoRL. DexBench and VABAR, two new open benchmarks, are among the first designed to measure robot dexterity and adaptability across industrial tasks using Isaac Lab-Arena and Newton.

DexBench, developed by RLWRLD with NVIDIA, takes dexterity evaluation off the tabletop and into real-world workflows, said the collaborators. Built using NVIDIA Isaac Lab-Arena, it features 15 tasks across four scenes spanning retail, logistics, manufacturing, and hospitality, testing generalization across object, spatial and physics variations.

Genesis AI, mimic robotics, and other industry partners are evaluating DexBench through early access. Teams can run DexBench on Manifold, Bifrost’s evaluation platform for scaling robotics simulations, with no setup required, built-in failure analysis and free credits for initial evaluations.

VABAR, the Variational Automation Benchmark for Agentic Robotics, from UC Berkeley and NVIDIA, evaluates robots across six industrial tasks. Each carries standardized variations, difficulty tiers, and success metrics.

How are robotics companies using NVIDIA technology?

Robotics developers are already putting NVIDIA’s latest technology to the test. A number of developers are using Isaac Lab 3.0 and Newton. At CoRL, Skild AI announced Scalable Throughput-optimized Engine for Embodied Learning, or STEEL, a new rigid-body physics solver built on Newton to accelerate robot training with Isaac Lab.

Flexion showcased how Isaac Lab and Newton help train Reflect, its robot-intelligence model combining reasoning and whole-body manipulation. FieldAI is using Newton, as well as Isaac Lab and Isaac Sim, to train and validate robot policies for deployment in unstructured real-world environments.

Dyna Robotics said it will demonstrate how parallel simulation in Isaac Lab helps train whole-body controllers for its semi-humanoid Taku robot for work in warehouses, hotels and food services.

Walden Robotics is using Isaac Sim’s photorealistic rendering to train and evaluate its general-purpose robot in virtual environments for manufacturing and logistics. Dexmate is exploring how coding agents can rehearse and refine manipulation strategies in Isaac Sim before executing them on its Vega robot.

AlphaNIST, built in Isaac Lab, demonstrates how efficient practice can translate into precision. A single policy learns all 20 tasks on the NIST Assembly Task Board, manipulating millimeter-scale parts using only a yes-or-no success signal. It achieves more than 98% training success, compared with 81% for separate per-task policies, using roughly 39x less GPU time.

Behind those results is Success-Guided Sampling, or SGS, from the University of Washington and NVIDIA. The method focuses practice on tasks a policy succeeds at about half the time, directing training toward skills it’s still learning. With SGS, robot training can scale beyond a million parallel environments.

The University of Texas at Austin’s School of Computing and Texas Robotics uses Isaac Sim and Isaac Lab to train robotic skills in simulation, letting students start developing before physical hardware is available.

item.title: Boston Dynamics adds wheels to Atlas humanoid to test whole-body control
item.dc:creator: Mike Oitzman
item.description:
Boston Dynamics combines classical motor control with whole-body reinforcement learning to power dynamic, wheeled locomotion for Atlas.

The post Boston Dynamics adds wheels to Atlas humanoid to test whole-body control appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Bridging the divide between deterministic physics-based control and policy-driven adaptation, Boston Dynamics released a video today showing its Atlas humanoid using wheels to move around. The “experiment” combined classical model-based motor control with whole-body reinforcement learning to maintain dynamic stability across unstructured, real-world terrain.

In the video, Andy Wu, controls engineer for Atlas at Boston Dynamics, highlights some recent experiments that he executed by attaching wheels to Atlas’ legs. Boston Dynamics said “a wheeled Atlas isn’t a product. It’s a research testbed.” Wu’s intention was to push the actuation to its limits.

Another goal of the experiment was to understand unstructured environment adaptability. Wu addresses the limitations of purely model-based control when navigating unpredictable, real-world conditions that are difficult to model or simulate.

Through a whole-body reinforcement learning (RL) policy, Atlas demonstrates that it can process real-time proprioceptive feedback and velocity commands. The experiment also outputs dynamic pose and force adjustments to mitigate unmodeled disturbances and non-ideal contact states.

Boston Dynamics attached wheels to the feet of the Atlas humanoid for a set of controls engineering experiments. | Credit: Boston Dynamics

Atlas moves like a skater

In addition to learning how to move with wheels for feet, Atlas also performs pirouettes and various aggressive actuation maneuvers.

This demonstrates that Atlas can smoothly switch between fast rolling on flat terrain and articulated legged motion over obstacles or irregular surfaces.

Wu trained the system in sim. The system learned all of the behaviors in sim and executed them in real life, with surprising accuracy, according to Wu.

Wu said converting Atlas’ locomotion style was “wonderfully simple.” A single custom adapter mounts an off-the-shelf scooter rim onto Atlas’ existing ankle actuator, and that’s the only new part in the whole build. Because Atlas was designed from the start to be produced at high volume and to be easy to service, Wu said the retrofit was about as involved as swapping a wheel on a bicycle.

The software side was just as straightforward, he said. Each wheel is modeled as an “ankle” that can spin continuously, so all Wu had to do was take the baseline robot model and swap the feet out for wheels.

Real-world implications for humanoid operation

The next question that Wu intends to answer is the policy response to failed actuators. This is key to safety and to understanding how the system will respond to a system failure.

The primary takeaway for Wu and the controls engineering team at Boston Dynamics is to understand control synergy. The video demonstrates that merging classical motor controls (for baseline stability) with whole-body RL (for reactive adaptation) yields superior real-world agility compared to using either method alone.

Wheels vs. legs debate continues

Boston Dynamics’ latest Atlas experiment adds another interesting data point to the ongoing wheels-versus-legs debate in humanoid robotics. While many companies are developing wheeled humanoids, others are committed to legs for navigating environments designed for people.

Agility Robotics recently said it is also exploring wheeled robots as part of a broader family of human-centric, multipurpose platforms. Co-founder and Chief Robot Officer Jonathan Hurst said Digit likely won’t get wheels, but the company is exploring other wheeled configurations.

Again, Boston Dynamics said a wheeled Atlas is a research testbed, not a product. Still, experiments like this raise an interesting question about how much of the humanoid form factor needs to be human-like to be commercially useful. We’ll be watching to see where the industry goes next.

The experiments come as Boston Dynamics prepares to ramp up Atlas testing at Hyundai facilities and continues developing the humanoid’s capabilities, including its new four-fingered gripper. The Robot Report will be watching how these developments translate into real-world deployments.

item.title: How to minimize Wi-Fi roaming interruptions for autonomous mobile robots
item.dc:creator: Mikko Niemi
item.description:
Dedicated Wi-Fi scan architectures can improve robot mobility, reliability, and performance, says Synaptics.

The post How to minimize Wi-Fi roaming interruptions for autonomous mobile robots appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
Wi-Fi connectivity needs to be reliable for real-time mobile robot management. Source: Synaptics

An autonomous mobile robot or AMR may cross dozens of Wi-Fi coverage zones during a single shift. Each transition creates a small but potentially consequential communications problem: How does the robot find its next access point without interrupting the connection it is already using?

The answer matters because AMRs, industrial inspection robots, warehouse automation, and healthcare service robots increasingly depend on continuous connectivity for sensor data, telemetry, and control.

In a conventional Wi-Fi architecture, the primary communication radio must periodically stop transmitting and receiving application traffic while it searches for alternative access points. That creates a tradeoff among connectivity, latency, power consumption, and roaming performance.

A dedicated scan architecture separates network discovery from application traffic. The robot can monitor its wireless environment continuously while the primary radio maintains the active connection.

One implementation, Synaptics Scan Core, uses a low-power wireless subsystem to monitor neighboring access points while the primary Wi-Fi radio remains dedicated to application traffic. This separation can support faster roaming decisions, lower latency, reduced packet loss, and more efficient scanning.

As robots become more mobile, roaming is mission-critical

Robots are becoming more connected and autonomous across manufacturing, logistics, healthcare, retail, and service environments. As they move through larger and more complex facilities, reliable wireless connectivity and fast roaming become core design requirements rather than secondary networking considerations.

Unlike stationary Wi-Fi devices, robots move continually between coverage areas while maintaining video, AI inference, telemetry, and fleet-management communications. These combined demands make mobile robotics a strong use case for dedicated scanning architectures.

Modern robots also support increasingly demanding wireless workloads, including HD and multi-camera video, simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM), AI-assisted navigation, predictive maintenance, and remote operation.

Wireless connectivity has therefore evolved from a convenience into a critical operational subsystem.

Submit your innovation now!

Mobility poses challenges

A mobile robot must maintain application traffic as it moves between Wi-Fi coverage zones. A warehouse robot may roam dozens or even hundreds of times during a shift. Each roaming event can introduce:

  • Increased latency
  • Packet loss
  • Video disruption
  • Delayed control responses
  • Reduced productivity

Common performance targets for robotics deployments include:

Requirement Typical Target
Roaming latency <80 ms
Sustained throughput 20 Mbps
Packet loss during roaming <2%

For many autonomous systems, meeting these targets is important to safe and efficient operation.

Key requirements and pain points

Although stakeholders evaluate robotics systems differently, several wireless performance measures consistently emerge as critical.

Roaming latency

A typical roaming process includes the following steps:

  1. Network discovery
  2. Candidate evaluation
  3. Authentication
  4. Security key exchange
  5. Reassociation

Each step adds delay. In robotics applications, excessive roaming latency can affect navigation, fleet coordination, teleoperation, and machine-vision performance.

Packet loss

Even brief connectivity interruptions can affect AMR operations and data transfer. Robots often require communications performance that is consistent and predictable enough for real-time operation.

Power consumption

AMRs must continuously balance battery performance and energy efficiency. Aggressive scanning improves roaming responsiveness but typically increases power consumption.

Dense RF environments

Warehouses, factories, airports, and hospitals often contain many access points, multiple wireless protocols, and significant RF reflections. These conditions place additional demands on roaming algorithms.

Dedicated scanning can address mobile robot connectivity

Traditional Wi-Fi clients use the primary communication radio for both application traffic and network discovery. During a background scan, the radio temporarily leaves its serving channel to look for neighboring access points, interrupting active traffic and potentially adding delay or packet loss.

A dedicated scan architecture assigns continuous monitoring of the wireless environment to a separate low-power resource. The primary Wi-Fi radio can remain focused on application traffic while candidate access points are identified in advance.

Source: Synaptics

Synaptics Scan Core is one implementation of this general architectural approach. A dedicated scan resource removes this contention between active communications and network discovery.

Source: Synaptics

Traditional Wi-Fi versus Scan Core

Conventional Wi-Fi Dedicated Scan Core
Main communication radio performs scanning Dedicated Scan Core performs scanning
User traffic interrupted during scans User traffic radio is not interrupted by scan operations
Reactive roaming Proactive roaming
Higher scan power Lower scan power
Longer roaming time Faster roaming
Periodic access point discovery Continuous AP discovery

Key benefits

  • Continuous network awareness: The scan radio continuously monitors neighboring channels while the primary radio remains connected.
  • Faster roaming decisions: Candidate access points are discovered before signal quality degrades.
  • Lower packet loss: Active communications continue during background scanning.
  • More predictable performance: Roaming behavior becomes more consistent and predictable.
  • Improved power efficiency: Background scanning can be optimized without disrupting active communications.

Instead of waiting for connectivity to deteriorate, the wireless subsystem can prepare for the next roaming event while application traffic continues on the primary radio.

Measured Scan Core benefits

Synaptics said its platform characterization measured substantial improvements in scanning efficiency:

Metric Improvement
Scan time Up to 65% faster
Overall scan duration Approximately 40% shorter
Scan power Up to 75% lower
Scan current Up to 77% lower

Source: Synaptics robotics platform characterization

In a mobile robot, these improvements can contribute to faster roaming, lower scan energy, longer battery life, and steadier application traffic. Actual results will depend on the platform, network topology, traffic load, and RF environment.

Applying dedicated scanning to mobile robots

Commercial connectivity platforms are beginning to incorporate dedicated scanning. For instance, Synaptics offers an integrated platform combining Wi-Fi 7, dual Bluetooth 6.0, and IEEE 802.15.4, as well as multi-band operation across 2.4, 5, and 6 GHz.

Within that platform, Scan Core provides a dedicated scan resource that operates independently of the primary WLAN subsystem. This allows scanning and active communications to occur simultaneously rather than compete for the same radio.

Multi-band awareness

The platform evaluates candidate access points across multiple frequency bands, helping the robot maintain connectivity as it moves through a facility.

Fast channel switching

The architecture supports rapid transitions between the main and scan resources. On the Synaptics robotics validation platform, switching between resources was measured on the order of microseconds.

Roaming test results

Figure 3 summarizes the minimum and maximum measured roaming times across three representative scenarios. In Synaptics platform testing, all results remained below the 80 ms target while continuous 20 Mbps UDP traffic was maintained:

Source: Synaptics

Wireless mobility becomes part of robot performance

As AMRs take on more complex workloads and operate across larger, denser environments, wireless mobility becomes part of the robot’s performance envelope. Roaming affects productivity, fleet efficiency, the user experience, and, in some applications, safe operation.

Conventional Wi-Fi makes the communication radio divide its time between application traffic and network discovery. A dedicated scan architecture separates those functions, allowing the robot to identify its next connection without interrupting the one it is already using.

Dedicated scanning and Wi-Fi 7 enhanced Multi-Link Single Radio (eMLSR) address different parts of wireless mobility. Dedicated scanning improves awareness of nearby access points; eMLSR improves how the device uses multiple links. Together, they can make roaming faster and more predictable without forcing designers to trade application performance against network awareness.

In Synaptics internal validation, eMLSR delivered up to a 10x latency improvement over single-link operation under congested conditions. Results vary with network topology, traffic load, and RF conditions. eMLSR can provide many multi-link operation latency benefits without requiring multiple fully active radios.

Synaptics says Scan Core can help mobile robots maintain coverage. Source: Synaptics

Glossary

Autonomous mobile robot An AMR can navigating and performing tasks using sensors, AI, and wireless connectivity without requiring fixed guidance infrastructure or direct human control.
Access point An AP is a wireless networking device that provides Wi-Fi connectivity to client devices within a coverage area.
Enhanced Multi-Link Single Radio eMLSR is a Wi-Fi 7 capability that enables a single radio to intelligently utilize multiple wireless links, improving latency, reliability, and power efficiency.
Fleet management Software and network infrastructure used to monitor, coordinate, and manage multiple AMRs operating within the same environment.
Latency The time required for data to travel between devices. Low and predictable latency is critical for real-time robotics applications.
Multi-Link Operation MLO is a Wi-Fi 7 feature that allows communication over multiple wireless links, improving throughput, reliability, and network efficiency.
Packet loss Data packets that fail to reach their destination. Excessive packet loss can interrupt video, telemetry, and real-time control.
Roaming The process by which a Wi-Fi client transitions from one access point to another while maintaining network connectivity.
Scan Core A dedicated low-power wireless receive subsystem that continuously monitors the wireless environment while the primary Wi-Fi radio remains dedicated to application traffic. By separating network awareness from communications, Scan Core enables faster roaming, lower latency, reduced packet loss, and improved power efficiency, according to Synaptics.
Simultaneous Localization and Mapping SLAM is a navigation technique that enables a robot to build a map of its environment while simultaneously determining its own position within that map.
Simultaneous Transmit and Receive STR is a Wi-Fi 7 Multi-Link Operation mode that enables simultaneous transmission and reception over multiple wireless links, maximizing throughput and reducing latency.
User Datagram Protocol UDP is a lightweight transport protocol used for real-time applications such as video streaming, voice, gaming, and telemetry. Unlike TCP, UDP does not retransmit lost packets, making it well suited for measuring network latency, packet loss, and roaming performance in wireless systems.
Wi-Fi 7  The latest generation of Wi-Fi technology (IEEE 802.11be) introduced features such as MLO, wider channel bandwidths, lower latency, and improved efficiency in dense wireless environments.

About the author

Mikko Niemi is a product manager for wireless products at Synaptics Inc. He has more than 15 years of experience across industrial Internet of Things (IIoT), semiconductor, and software-as-a-service (SaaS) sectors. Niemi specializes in building and scaling intelligent, data-driven platforms that power connected infrastructure, smart energy systems, and next-generation industrial applications.

He previously worked at Lantronix, where he led a portfolio that included industrial IoT gateways, cloud-based, SaaS device management platforms, and global connectivity services—delivering edge-to-cloud systems that integrate real-time telemetry, AI/machine learning analytics, and robust security at scale. Niemi previosly held management roles at Silicon Labs and Landis+Gyr. He holds an MBA and a Master’s in electronics engineering.

item.title: ARM Institute consortium grows to more than 500 organizations
item.dc:creator: The Robot Report Staff
item.description:
The ARM Institute reached the milestone as it prepares to host its 10th annual member meeting in Pittsburgh.

The post ARM Institute consortium grows to more than 500 organizations appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
The annual ARM Institute member meeting takes place in Pittsburgh. Source: ARM Institute

The Advanced Robotics for Manufacturing, or ARM Institute last week said that that its member consortium has grown to include more than 500 organizations nationwide, with thousands of individual subject matter experts represented within these organizations. The organization collaborates with its consortium and the U.S. government to promote the U.S. as leading nation in manufacturing output through the adoption of robotics and AI.

“We are proud to work with our consortium to build a resilient, secure, and bright future for U.S. manufacturing,” stated Jorgen Pedersen, CEO of the ARM Institute. “Our member consortium is the foundation of our Institute and integral to our mission.”

“Our members have collaborated with us on hundreds of technology projects, helped us launch major initiatives, including our national workforce resource RoboticsCareer.org, supported manufacturers through their robotics and automation journey, and more,” he added. “We look forward to celebrating this milestone at our 10th Annual Member Meeting later this month.”

Founded in 2017, the ARM Institute is a Manufacturing Innovation Institute (MII) funded by the Office of the Secretary of War under Agreement No. W911NF-17-3-0004 and is part of the Manufacturing USA network. The organization relies on its member consortium and partners across industry, academia, and government to promote U.S. manufacturing leadership through the adoption of robotics and AI.

ARM Institute conducts activities with and for members

The ARM Institute said it focuses on catalyzing innovative yet practical robotics and physical AI solutions. The Pittsburg-based institute said it is also working to grow and prepare the U.S. workforce for advanced manufacturing careers.

“The ARM Institute’s member consortium is expansive, bridging gaps and bringing varied perspectives together to catalyze robotics, physical AI, and workforce solutions to strengthen U.S. manufacturing,” stated the organization.

Last month, the institute issued a project call from the U.S. Navy to address needs in the shipbuilding industrial base. This month, the ARM Institute put out a request for proposals for a skills gap analysis for a localized talent supply chain to support the organic and defense industrial base.

Its consortium members include manufacturers of all sizes, defense contractors, technology providers offering robotics and AI systems, research universities, community colleges, vocational schools, government entities, startups, and others.

ARM Institute membership is at the organizational level and provides access to funding opportunities, member-exclusive events, a digital member community for virtual collaboration, and more. Companies, governmental bodies, and educational institutions that otherwise would be considered competitors work together through the institute for the benefit of the nation and manufacturers across the U.S., asserted the organization.

10th annual member meeting coming soon

The ARM Institute marked the membership milestone as it prepares to host its 10th Annual Member Meeting from Nov. 17 to 19. This member-exclusive event convenes experts from across ARM’s consortium and the U.S. government for two and a half days of networking, collaboration, and knowledge-sharing.

The event in Pittsburgh will feature expert-led presentations, networking and curated matchmaking, a Member Showcase Hall, and more. This year’s event will feature celebratory content and activities in recognition of the anniversary.

Registration for the ARM Institute’s 2026 Annual Member Meeting closes on Nov. 13. Register or join the ARM Member Consortium before then to gain access to the meeting.

item.title: Robot integration brings high-precision production to midmarket manufacturers
item.dc:creator: Lou Farrell
item.description:
Properly integrated industrial and collaborative robots can help midmarket manufacturers, according to a columnist.

The post Robot integration brings high-precision production to midmarket manufacturers appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
High-precision manufacturing was once considered something exclusive to large corporations. However, advances in robotic integration and automated manufacturing have changed this perception.

Sophisticated capabilities are becoming accessible to midmarket and smaller operations. This shift has led to a more even competitive landscape.

Smaller manufacturers have an opportunity to reach new levels of accuracy and efficiency. Today’s robotic systems can help these producers modernize targeted workflows without overhauling their entire production operations.

Robotic innovations drive efficiency for manufacturers

The evolution of robotics has led to more democratized precision manufacturing processes. This is evident across industrial robots and agile collaborative robots.

Key benefits of these innovations can include:

  • Cost and footprint: The potential for lower investment costs and compact designs can make robotic systems economically viable. It can also simplify integration into existing layouts.
  • Enhanced programming: Intuitive interfaces and lead-through teaching methods support quick deployment and reconfiguration. This reduces the training typically required for operators without robotics expertise.
  • Sensors and AI-driven capabilities: Sensors, such as vision systems and force-torque sensors, can be integrated with AI. This enables robots to understand, react and adapt with precision.
  • Safety and collaboration: Cobots can work safely alongside humans without extensive guarding. This fosters a flexible human-robot workforce that combines optimal utilization and human dexterity.

These advancements mean that midmarket manufacturers can overcome hurdles like skilled labor shortages, rising costs, and quality demands.

Submit your innovation now!

Real-world impact of robotic integration for precision manufacturers

Here are some use cases that show how a diverse range of manufacturers have taken advantage of recent advances in robotics.

1. SCHUNK R-C2 automation for flexible production

Torneria Novoletto is an Italian organization specializing in sophisticated components for the chemical, medical, and pharmaceutical sectors.

The company faced obstacles in achieving high precision and process reliability for medium-sized batches. It implemented SCHUNK’s R-C2 automation concept, integrating advanced clamping devices and grippers with robotic handling.

Introducing this system helped to support high operational flexibility. Setup and changeover times were also significantly reduced because the SCHUNK R-C2 allows the continuous handling of workpiece sizes and automated reclamping.

This innovative robotic integration has helped Torneria Novoletto to pursue an unmanned 24/7 operation, increase machine utilization, and mitigate shortages of skilled labor.

Torneria Novoletto shows the compact efficiency of the R-C2 automation. Source: SCHUNK

2. Cobot integration for part marking

Telesis, a leading provider of industrial marking solutions, integrated its part marking technology with systems from Universal Robots.

The company offers advanced laser and dot peen markers. When a Telesis laser marking system is integrated with a UR force- and power-limited robot arm, it creates a precise and flexible method of identifying automated parts.

Innovations like this ensure that systems can be safely deployed alongside human workers. Robotic integrations have provided Telesis with a streamlined marking process without complex safety enclosures, consistent high-quality marking on various materials and part geometries, and added traceability and quality control.

Telesis demonstrates integrated laser-marking systems with robotic control. Source: Universal Robots

3. FANUC M-20 robots enhance throughput and scale

Northern Kentucky Machine (NKM), a flexible job shop, experienced labor shortages and production capacity challenges. Its strategic response included the use of automated manufacturing solutions, such as deploying FANUC M-20 Series industrial robots.

By using Automation Within Reach’s (AWR) “RC-2” CNC machine-tending system, the integration increased NKM’s throughput and machine utilization.

Operators quickly adapted to programming and running these robotic cells. This helped to enable “lights-out” manufacturing for longer runs, freeing up human workers for other tasks.

The FANUC robots have provided NKM with the scalability needed to pursue and take on larger projects, deliver consistent part quality, drive growth, and compete with other midsize organizations.

NKM used the M-20 Series robot to boost the efficiency of human workers. Source: FANUC

4. ActiNav enables bin picking and legacy equipment extension

PrecisionForm Inc. is a producer of small custom metal parts. It faced the challenge of automating bin picking for CNC machines.

By deploying Universal Robots’ ActiNav system, PrecisionForm integrated a UR5 cobot with advanced vision and path-planning capabilities. This approach led to reliable part picking from deep bins that were then loaded into CNC machines.

Challenging geometries were less of an issue, and operators were freed up to manage multiple machines. The UR cobots helped reduce labor challenges and extend the lifespan of older CNC equipment.

By adding a relatively inexpensive robotic solution, PrecisionForm Inc gained additional utility from existing machinery, increased the potential return on investment (ROI) as a midmarket operation, and improved daily production.

Uses can easily deploy and calibrate the ActiNav system, says UR. Source: Universal Robots

Capabilities evolve for midmarket manufacturers

The accessibility of precision manufacturing marks a crucial moment for many industries. Robotic integration is no longer exclusive to the world’s largest enterprises.

Innovations offering ultra-high accuracy and consistent quality are now economically and operationally viable for midsized manufacturers. The benefits that organizations such as Telesis, Torneria Novoletto, NKM, and PrecisionForm now have shown that modern robotics can drive sustainable growth.

Robotic solutions continue to evolve. As they do, the advantages of automated manufacturing will grow alongside those changes. With thoughtful and careful implementation, a new generation of agile and highly precise manufacturers will be waiting to reap the benefits of this exciting new world.

About the author

Lou Farrell, a senior editor at Revolutionized, has written on the topics of robotics, computing, and technology for years. He has a great passion for the stories he covers and for writing in general.
