item.title: Boston Dynamics built Stretch Gen 2 for reliable, consistent performance
item.dc:creator: Brianna Wessling
item.description:
Brian Donnelly, the VP and GM of logistics robotics at Boston Dynamics, said the new version of Stretch has been in the works for two and a half years. 

The post Boston Dynamics built Stretch Gen 2 for reliable, consistent performance appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
The new Stretch features an updated modular design that enables “plug and play” part swaps. | Source: Boston Dynamics

Boston Dynamics Inc. this week unveiled Stretch Gen 2, the latest generation of its autonomous mobile trailer unloading robot. With over 100,000 operating hours and tens of millions of boxes handled under its belt, the company built the updated robot to maximize uptime and streamline maintenance.

Brian Donnelly, the vice president and general manager of logistics robotics at Boston Dynamics, told The Robot Report that the company has been working on the new version of Stretch for around two and a half years.

“When we made the first generation of Stretch, we were focused on trying to get a product out into the market as fast as possible and really get it in customers’ hands and get it operational,” he said. “It was not the easiest to manufacture; there were a lot of components.”

“[With Stretch 2], we really were focused on simplification, hardening the robot, and really driving improved reliability and performance,” added Donnelly. “That’s really what drove a lot of our decisions was just making the robot better in every way.”

Stretch Gen 2 can unload up to 1,000 cases per hour. This rate is highly dependent on factors such as case weight and how neat or disorderly cases are stacked. It has a multipick feature, a battery that can last two shifts, and a fast charger that can get it to 90% charge in about 75 minutes.

The mobile manipulator also features onboard lighting, making it easier to work in dark trailers, and a pre-trained vision system that can detect most packages without programming needed.

Stretch’s hardware upgrades improve durability

Boston Dynamics geared many of Stretch Gen 2’s upgrades towards reducing downtime and making the robot more durable. For example, the Waltham, Mass.-based company also cut 81% of the internal cabling, around half a mile’s worth.

“[Cabling] is weight, it’s cost, and its points of failure, particularly when you have something that’s in constant motion, you’re creating strain on those cables with every motion,” Donnelly said. “If you don’t have good strain relief, you don’t have good ways of managing the cables in the robot. It can cause stress on the cables and then failure.”

Donnelly said Hyundai helped the company source a cable harness through its automotive supply chain. This isn’t the only thing Boston Dynamics learned from the automotive industry. Stretch Gen 2 uses heavy-duty automotive-grade connectors. These hold up to the vibration of rapid, high-torque box handling and driving over uneven floors.

“In the automotive industry, they have to deal with a lot of real-world challenges in their vehicles. There’s a lot of miles driven dealing with shock and vibration and things like this,” Donnelly said. “As a robot moves around the world, just like a car, if you don’t have latching connectors, then they can sort of wiggle apart. By leveraging those automotive connectors, we’re much more confident that the connectors are going to stay latched together and not pull apart in the field.”

The robot also has continuous rotation joints that move beyond 360° so they no longer hit hard stops. This can help prevent previously caused mechanical stress. Donnelly pointed out this also makes the robot more productive, as it can completely optimize its trajectory planning and move in any direction.

The emergency stop on the robot now sits lower and is recessed. Boston Dynamics made the exterior panels with new materials so a falling box is far less likely to trip an unintentional safety stoppage or break a panel.

How Stretch Gen 2 gets a grip on multiple boxes

The gripper is the part of the robot that often deals with the most stress. It’s making contact with all of the the things the robot needs to handle. Stretch Gen 2 features an upgraded gripper with new valve systems and more precise sensing improves grasping and placement to optimize fast-paced picks.

“[The new gripper] has a valve in every suction cup, which enables us to pick multiple boxes with a single motion of the arm, which substantially increases our throughput,” Donnelly explained. “If we can pick multiple boxes, with a single motion of the arm, we get much higher throughput because the pick cycle of picking up a box from the floor of a container and place it to a conveyor is dominated by arm movement. So, if we can keep the arm moving and just do more every cycle, that is really effective and improves the rate at which we can unload a truck for our customers.”

The new gripper is also better at configuring boxes on the conveyor belt in ways that work best for Boston Dynamics’ customers, and use less power in picking up boxes.

“Every cup is individually sensed and actuated, so we know when we have good suction,” said Donnelly. “We only have the valve open to pull suction when we have good contact on a box, so that enables us to reduce the amount of power we’re spending running on the vacuum pump, so we’re not pulling suction through cups that don’t have good contact. It also enables us to, when we pick up those multiple boxes, singulate them onto the conveyor.”

Stretch Gen 2 brings service time down to just hours

With Stretch Gen 2, Boston Dynamics didn’t just want to reduce the frequency of service calls; it also wanted to make those service calls faster when they do happen.

“We didn’t have as much experience from a serviceability perspective as a company when we made the first-generation robot,” Donnelly said. “We’ve since deployed these robots, serviced them in the field, and hired a lot of people who have a lot more experience than we originally did in service. Their input and guidance really helped us to make a robot that’s much more manufacturable and more serviceable.”

The robot doesn’t require dynamic cables and complex harnesses. Instead it uses standardized high-strength fasteners to cut down on tool changes and hands-on repair time. For example, the company can perform a full swerve drive swap in just one hour. Before, this process could take an entire day.

Stretch Gen 2 also features new onboard diagnostics and maintenance tools. These put more routine service in the hands of a customer’s own maintenance team, so robots stay on the dock with less reliance on outside support.

Updated robot continuously improves its performance

The new robot runs on a redesigned onboard computing platform that is constantly improving. Boston Dynamics said it will regularly release software updates to bring gains in case detection, motion planning, pick strategies, and world modeling across an entire fleet, with no hardware changes required.

Donnelly said that with the company’s most recent update, it saw a 24% increase in unload rate across its fleet of fielded robots.

“A lot of our activity on this program is really focused on the software. We’re constantly improving our computer vision capabilities to be able to better perceive boxes and conveyors and container walls, and then really pick boxes and place them to convey more and more productivity over time,” Donnelly said.

Right now, Donnelly said Boston Dynamics releases new software, on average, on a monthly basis.

How have customers reacted to Gen 2 so far?

Donnelly said Boston Dynamics already has Stretch Gen 2 running at multiple customer sites.

“Customers are really happy with it, and they’re continuing to rely on it to do its work every day,” said Donnelly. “We’re going into these existing sites and deploying these robots within two weeks. The folks who are taking over operating the robots are the folks who are otherwise doing repetitive heavy lifting of these boxes and containers.”

“We put a lot of effort into ensuring that the user experience, from an operator perspective, is really simple. It doesn’t require a ton of training,” he added. “A person can drive the robot into a container, step out of the safety work cell, and they press a big Play button, and then the robot does the rest.”

Many of the people working with Stretch used to spend their days unloading heavy boxes from trailers.

“Fundamentally, unloading trailers is one of the worst jobs in the warehouse,” Donnelly said. “It can be really hot in a container that’s been sitting in a yard in the summer. It can be super cold in the winter. Then the work itself is moving heavy boxes repeatedly from down low or up high. It puts a lot of strain and stress on people’s bodies.”

The post Boston Dynamics built Stretch Gen 2 for reliable, consistent performance appeared first on The Robot Report.

item.title: Industry experts discuss China blocking SoftBank acquisition of ABB Robotics
item.dc:creator: Eugene Demaitre
item.description:
China's prohibition of SoftBank's purchase of ABB Robotics reflects wider concerns about data and AI, say experts.

The post Industry experts discuss China blocking SoftBank acquisition of ABB Robotics appeared first on The Robot Report.
item.ns3:encoded:
ABB Robotics has integrated NVIDIA Omniverse libraries into RobotStudio. Source: ABB Robotics

Yesterday, ABB Robotics confirmed to The Robot Report that China’s Office of the Working Mechanism for Foreign Investment Security Review has blocked SoftBank Group Corp.’s planned acquisition of ABB Robotics. Regulators had expressed concern that data for training artificial intelligence models could be transferred overseas.

ABB Robotics is already a significant manufacturer and provider of robotics in China. The Zurich-based company stated that it and SoftBank are “in close dialogue and are working constructively on the transaction.”

Other countries are moving to protect what they view as sovereign physical AI. For instance, the U.S. Federal Communications Commission (FCC) recently banned new models of certain connected advanced devices, including legged robots and autonomous mobile robots (AMRs). Companies such as Intel and Husqvarna have already received conditional approvals.

In addition, the U.S. Department of Commerce last week determined that imports of robotics, industrial machinery, and related components pose a threat to the U.S. economy and national security. This could lead to tariffs.

Government investigations can directly affect major robotics and AI companies. European antitrust scrutiny of Amazon’s proposed acquisition of iRobot was one reason why that deal was terminated, with iRobot subsequently entering bankruptcy proceedings. The robotic vacuum pioneer has since been picked up by Shenzhen, China-based Picea Robotics Co.

ABB Robotics as focused on automation and AI

ABB Robotics claimed that it is the only company whose integrated portfolio includes industrial automation, software, force- and power-limited cobots, and AMRs. The company said its “autonomous versatile robotics” help businesses of all sizes in industries including automotive, electronics, and logistics.

ABB Robotics has installed more than 500,000 robots around the world and employs about 7,000 people. Its U.S. headquarters are in Auburn Hills, Mich. In October 2025, parent company ABB said it had agreed to sell its robotics division to Japan-based SoftBank Group Corp. for $5.3 billion.

“Considering the intensive competition in traditional robotics, established manufacturers like ABB will need to lead the charge in AI-driven robotics to protect their margins,” said Samantha Mou, a senior analyst at Interact Analysis. “However, achieving this will require significant investment. The substantial long-term R&D costs may be a key factor behind ABB’s decision to sell its robotics business.”

“Compared with the other Big 4 vendors [FANUC, KUKA, and Yaskawa], ABB was already quick in combining AI with its products, which is an area where it can have synergy with SoftBank,” Mou told The Robot Report. She said that companies in Europe, Asia, and the Americas are hoping that AI, which has already been used for ease of programming, monitoring, and predictive maintenance, can be generalized to more processes.

“AI gives ABB Robotics considerable potential,” said Robert Little, a business development advisor and former chief of robotics strategy at Novanta Inc, on LinkedIn. “But turning that potential into commercially useful systems requires sustained investment. In my humble opinion, backing that investment within ABB becomes a harder decision when robotics has to compete for funding against higher-margin businesses. ABB also saw limited synergies between robotics and the rest of the company.”

“SoftBank made sense,” he added. “ABB brings robot manufacturing, application expertise and established customer relationships. SoftBank could bring additional investment and a clear focus on AI.”

Sovereign physical AI becomes a strategic concern

“Post Astra, robotics data has become more strategic,” posted Financial Times reporter Zijing Wu, in reference to the GPT-6 model that OpenAI released in September and that Chinese AI firms used to train their models.

“The NDRC [China’s National Development and Reform Commission] had been concerned about robotics data being transferred overseas, where it could be used to train AI models, including those developed by OpenAI, in which SoftBank is a major investor, sources say,” said Wu on X.

Countries have become increasingly aware of the competitive advantage promised by the convergence of automation and AI.

“What makes this particularly significant is that industrial robotics is increasingly being viewed not simply as manufacturing equipment, but as strategically important technology at the intersection of automation, data, and AI,” Ash Sharma, managing director of Interact Analysis, told The Robot Report.

“China is a critical market for ABB Robotics, so separating the Chinese operation from a global transaction of this scale would be extremely challenging,” he added. “More broadly, this highlights how robotics data, intellectual property, and local manufacturing capability are becoming important considerations in cross-border M&A as physical AI develops.”

Ahmed Humayun, head of go to market for defense manufacturing at Gecko Robotics, posted to LinkedIn: “This move reflects Chinese concerns about asset transfers to Japan during a time of heightened Chinese-Japanese tension, but [it] also shows concerns about robotics data generated in China being transferred abroad to train foundation models. The most recent example of China flexing its economic muscle and demonstrating that it has many levers to prevent intellectual property and assets from leaving its soil — even when developed by foreign companies.”

“I was worried this might happen,” said Little. “Over the years, I have seen ABB‘s strength in China grow. Where do we go from here?”

“My take: ABB has built a strong presence in China, but heavily subsidized Chinese robot makers are becoming stronger competitors at home and expanding into Europe,” he wrote. “That creates more pressure on pricing and margins that were not that great to begin with fall even further.”

“There may still be negotiations that find a way forward,” concluded Little. “For now, ABB is in a pickle.”
